lessons.title: Progression that skips the dominant
explanation: Common-practice function reports to a dominant that wants to resolve. Non-functional writing does not. Roots may sit, slide, or loop without owing V a cadence. The chain is still harmony. It just never clocks in as V–I.
MIT 21M.350 asks what the piece actually does. If the guitar never plays a dominant, do not invent one on the page. Write a loop of cells. Analyze the loop. Leave the missing V out of the report.
lessons.example: Power-chord loop E–C–Bb–C, four bars, no V of E. Calling it i–VI–bV–VI invents a key contract the riff never signed. Name the cells and the return.
lessons.whyItMatters: Invent a missing dominant and you will hear a cadence that is not on the tape.

quiz.stem: Non-functional harmony is a progression that does which of these jobs?
quiz.correctAnswer: Moves without reporting to a dominant that must resolve

distractors.text: Reports every root to a hidden V–I the page must invent
distractors.rationale: Inventing V–I is the habit this lesson refuses.

distractors.text: Ranks chords by how stable a textbook says they feel
distractors.rationale: Stability ranks are not the job here.

distractors.text: Deletes pitch so only the kit can carry the form
distractors.rationale: The letters still move. They just skip V.

quiz.correctExplanation: The chain can still move. It does not clock in with V–I.
objectiveIds: Write a progression that does not report to a dominant

quiz.stem: A riff loops E5–C5–Bb5 and never plays a B chord. Honest analysis should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Name the cells and the return without inventing a V–I

distractors.text: Insert a silent B7 so the loop can count as a cadence
distractors.rationale: No B7 is on the tape. Do not invent one.

distractors.text: Call the loop unfinished until someone adds a leading tone
distractors.rationale: The loop already closed by return.

distractors.text: Treat the letters as a drum fill with no harmonic claim
distractors.rationale: The cells are the harmony. Report them.

quiz.correctExplanation: No dominant appears. Do not smuggle one in to finish a textbook sentence.
objectiveIds: Analyze it without inventing a V–I that is not there

quiz.stem: You need four bars that do not report to a dominant. Which loop keeps that contract?
quiz.correctAnswer: E5–C5–G5–F5 returning to E5 with no B chord

distractors.text: E5–B7–E5–B7, because V–I is required for any loop
distractors.rationale: That loop reports to a dominant on purpose.

distractors.text: E5 then a rest, because harmony is illegal without V
distractors.rationale: Harmony can move without V. Write the cells.

distractors.text: B7–E5 only, relabeled as non-functional because it is loud
distractors.rationale: Loudness does not cancel a cadence.

quiz.correctExplanation: Roots that return without a dominant still make a progression.
objectiveIds: Write a progression that does not report to a dominant

lessons.title: Harmony that refuses a dominant
explanation: Functional labels assume a dominant that points home. Drop that assumption and the same letters can still move. Adjacent roots, modal oscillation, and color jumps are progressions. They are not failed V–I. They are a different job.

Analysis that invents a missing dominant is a chorale habit. MIT 21M.350 starts from what repeats and what contrasts. If no V appears, do not smuggle one in to complete a textbook sentence. Report the cells that are actually struck.

Write a four-bar loop whose roots never form a dominant of the home pitch. Then refuse the rescue: do not add a B7 at the end to make it resolve. The loop already closed by returning to the first cell.
lessons.example: E5 for a bar, C5 for a bar, Bb5 for a bar, back to E5. No B7. The return is the close. A Roman-numeral rescue that inserts V is a paper cadence, not the riff.
lessons.whyItMatters: Force V–I onto a riff that refused it and every later label will describe a piece nobody played.

quiz.stem: A loop of adjacent roots with no dominant is best named as which object?
quiz.correctAnswer: A progression that does a different job than V–I

distractors.text: A broken cadence waiting for someone to add V
distractors.rationale: The job is not a missing handshake.

distractors.text: A drum pattern that cannot carry pitch at all
distractors.rationale: The letters are still harmonic cells.

distractors.text: A key change that must pass through a pivot chord
distractors.rationale: A loop of cells is not a pivot modulation.

quiz.correctExplanation: Adjacent roots and color jumps are still progressions. They skip the dominant report.
objectiveIds: Write a progression that does not report to a dominant

quiz.stem: The tape never plays a dominant of E, but a chart writes V–I anyway. You should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Drop the invented V–I and report the cells that sound

distractors.text: Keep V–I because every riff secretly cadences offstage
distractors.rationale: Offstage cadences are the habit, not the tape.

distractors.text: Delete the pitch names so the chart has no harmony
distractors.rationale: The cells are the harmony. Keep their letters.

distractors.text: Move the riff into a new key until a dominant appears
distractors.rationale: Changing key to find V is another invention.

quiz.correctExplanation: MIT 21M.350 starts from what is there. Invented V–I is not there.
objectiveIds: Analyze it without inventing a V–I that is not there

quiz.stem: Write four bars on E that refuse a dominant. Which ending keeps the contract?
quiz.correctAnswer: Return to the first E cell with no B chord added

distractors.text: Add B7 on the last beat so a textbook can call it a cadence
distractors.rationale: That is the rescue this lesson refuses.

distractors.text: End on rest because a loop without V is not harmony
distractors.rationale: Return is already a close.

distractors.text: Jump to B major and stay there as a new tonic forever
distractors.rationale: A new tonic is a different claim, not this loop.

quiz.correctExplanation: The return closes the loop. A last-second B7 would hire V after the fact.
objectiveIds: Write a progression that does not report to a dominant

lessons.title: Slide the shape, keep the intervals
explanation: Slide a voicing so every voice moves the same distance. The intervals inside the shape stay. Function does not, because the new bass is a new root, not a voice-leading correction. That parallel move is the harmony.

Species writing treats consecutive perfect fifths as an error to fix. Planing treats them as the event. Debussy's parallel stacks and a guitarist's sliding power-chord shape share the mechanism: a rigid interval set that travels.

Write E5–F5–G5 as one fingerboard shape moving by step. Do not fix the fifths by contrary motion. The parallel fifths are the riff. Calling them a voice-leading mistake names a rule the music did not hire.
lessons.example: One finger bars E5, slides to F5, then Gb5. Each attack is a perfect fifth. Nothing contrary-motions the fifths apart. The slide is the progression.
lessons.whyItMatters: Correct the fifths and you erase the piece. Name the parallel move as the harmony, then decide whether you wanted that piece.

quiz.stem: Planing is the move where a chord shape does which of these things?
quiz.correctAnswer: Slides so inner intervals stay while function does not

distractors.text: Holds one common tone while neighbors step in contrary motion
distractors.rationale: That is ordinary voice leading, not planing.

distractors.text: Fixes consecutive fifths by rewriting them as thirds
distractors.rationale: Planing keeps the fifths. It does not fix them.

distractors.text: Deletes the bass so only an inner voice can move
distractors.rationale: The whole shape travels, bass included.

quiz.correctExplanation: Rigid intervals, new root. Function is not the cargo.
objectiveIds: Slide a shape so the intervals stay and the function does not

quiz.stem: A guitar slides a power-chord shape up two frets. The honest harmonic claim is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A parallel move that is the harmony, not a voice-leading error

distractors.text: A species mistake that must be rewritten in contrary motion
distractors.rationale: The parallel fifths are the event.

distractors.text: A modulation that secretly hired a dominant of the new fret
distractors.rationale: A slide is not a cadence into a new key.

distractors.text: A loudness swell that only looks like pitch motion
distractors.rationale: The frets moved. Pitch moved.

quiz.correctExplanation: The shape traveled. That travel is the progression.
objectiveIds: Write a parallel move that is the harmony, not a voice-leading error

quiz.stem: Someone 'corrects' sliding E5–F5–G5 into contrary fifths. What did they erase?
quiz.correctAnswer: The parallel shape whose intervals were the riff

distractors.text: A missing V–I that the slide had been hiding all along
distractors.rationale: The slide was not a hidden cadence.

distractors.text: Only the timbre, because parallel motion cannot carry pitch
distractors.rationale: The letters moved with the shape.

distractors.text: The barline, which is the only thing a slide can change
distractors.rationale: The slide changed pitch, not the meter grid.

quiz.correctExplanation: Fixing the fifths deletes the mechanism. The parallel stack was the harmony.
objectiveIds: Write a parallel move that is the harmony, not a voice-leading error

lessons.title: Roots a third apart, few shared tones
explanation: Chromatic mediants put roots a third apart with few common tones and a sudden color change. C major to E major shares one pitch class. C major to A-flat major shares one. The ear hears a jump, not a pivot chord earning the new key.

Common-practice modulation often borrows a chord that belongs to both keys. This jump skips that paperwork. MIT 21M.302 still names the third-relation; a riff uses it as a cut: E minor to C major, or C5 to E5, without a German sixth doing the work.

Connect E5 to C5, or E major to C major, and sit on the new color. Do not add a pivot ii–V to explain the arrival. The color is the third-relation itself. Hear the few shared tones, then the new root.
lessons.example: Bar of E major, bar of C major, back. One shared pitch class. No A minor pivot, no B7. The jump is the event. The few common tones are the seam.
lessons.whyItMatters: Force a pivot and you will miss the cut. The color is the third, not the paperwork you wished had been there.

quiz.stem: Chromatic mediants connect which pair of roots, and with what kind of overlap?
quiz.correctAnswer: Roots a third apart, with few common tones and a color jump

distractors.text: Roots a fifth apart, with a dominant that must resolve
distractors.rationale: A fifth with V is ordinary function, not this jump.

distractors.text: The same root twice, with every tone held in common
distractors.rationale: Few common tones are the point, not a freeze.

distractors.text: Any two power chords, because loudness is the mediant
distractors.rationale: The relation is a third between roots.

quiz.correctExplanation: A third between roots, a thin seam of shared tones, a color cut.
objectiveIds: Connect roots a third apart with few common tones

quiz.stem: E major cuts to C major with no pivot. The honest hearing of that jump is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A color change from the third-relation, not a earned modulation

distractors.text: A failed cadence that still owes the listener a B7
distractors.rationale: The jump did not hire V. Do not collect the debt.

distractors.text: A secret pivot through A minor that the tape omitted
distractors.rationale: An omitted pivot is an invented one.

distractors.text: A meter change, because color jumps can only be rhythmic
distractors.rationale: The letters changed. Meter can sit still.

quiz.correctExplanation: Hear the few shared tones and the new root. That is the color.
objectiveIds: Hear the color of that jump without forcing a pivot

quiz.stem: You want the mediant color without forcing a pivot. Which move keeps the contract?
quiz.correctAnswer: Strike E5 then C5 and sit, with no ii–V into C

distractors.text: Strike E5, then ii–V of C, then C, so a textbook can explain it
distractors.rationale: The ii–V is the paperwork this lesson skips.

distractors.text: Strike E5 then F5, calling any step a chromatic mediant
distractors.rationale: A step is not a third between roots.

distractors.text: Mute both chords so the color exists only as a rest
distractors.rationale: The jump needs the two roots sounding.

quiz.correctExplanation: Two roots a third apart, thin overlap, no pivot hired.
objectiveIds: Connect roots a third apart with few common tones

lessons.title: Six semitones as a relation
explanation: Six semitones split the octave in half. That interval is a relation you can aim: E against B-flat, A against E-flat. Treat it as a cell, a substitution, or a polarity, not as a wrong fifth that slipped into the take.

Tritone substitution in common-practice craft replaces V with a dominant a tritone away, because they share the third and seventh. A riff can skip that story and grind the two pitches as a two-note cell. Both uses are on purpose.

Write E–Bb as a repeating cell, or swap a B7 for an F7 before E. Name the relation. Do not call the tritone an accident of distortion or a mood. It is six frets, a geometric fact, and a harmonic choice.
lessons.example: Palm-muted E and Bb on one string, two-bar cell. Or last bar of a phrase: F7 instead of B7 into E. Same six-semitone relation, two jobs: cell versus substitution.
lessons.whyItMatters: Call the tritone an accident and you will not be able to write it twice on purpose. Name the split octave, then choose the job.

quiz.stem: The tritone is best treated as which of these harmonic facts?
quiz.correctAnswer: The interval that bisects the octave, aimed as a relation

distractors.text: A wrong fifth that distortion always inserts by accident
distractors.rationale: Six frets is a choice, not a glitch.

distractors.text: A duration mark that splits a whole note into two halves
distractors.rationale: The split is pitch, not note length.

distractors.text: A loudness pair that must be played at the same forte
distractors.rationale: The relation is interval size, not energy.

quiz.correctExplanation: Six semitones. Half the octave. A relation you can write.
objectiveIds: Use the interval that bisects the octave as a relation, not an accident

quiz.stem: You want the tritone on purpose in a riff. Which writing keeps that contract?
quiz.correctAnswer: Repeat E against Bb as a cell, or swap F7 for B7 into E

distractors.text: Avoid E and Bb because the interval is illegal in any riff
distractors.rationale: The point is to write it, not ban it.

distractors.text: Raise the mix fader until a fifth starts to sound like six semitones
distractors.rationale: Loudness does not retune the interval.

distractors.text: Write only E5 power chords so no other interval can appear
distractors.rationale: A stack of fifths is a different cell.

quiz.correctExplanation: Cell or substitution. Either way the six-semitone relation is aimed.
objectiveIds: Write a tritone substitution or a tritone riff cell on purpose

quiz.stem: A chart labels E–Bb as a slipped fifth from distortion. The better name is:
quiz.correctAnswer: A tritone relation written as a cell, not an accident

distractors.text: A dominant of E that is hiding inside the two notes
distractors.rationale: E and Bb are not automatically V of E.

distractors.text: A rest, because tritones cannot be harmonic material
distractors.rationale: They are material. The cell is the harmony.

distractors.text: A pivot chord that modulates by splitting the barline
distractors.rationale: The interval is a pitch relation, not a meter trick.

quiz.correctExplanation: Name the split octave. Then you can repeat it on purpose.
objectiveIds: Use the interval that bisects the octave as a relation, not an accident

lessons.title: Home on a diminished triad
explanation: Locrian builds a tonic triad that is already diminished: root, minor third, diminished fifth. Sitting on that tonic means home is unstable by construction. The mode is useful as color because the home chord contains a tritone from the first stack.

Predict the itch: the ear wants to hear that diminished tonic as vii° of somewhere else, usually the relative major. If you keep returning to the pitch as 1, you are in Locrian. If you cadence in the relative, you left the mode.

Write a figure that keeps B as 1 with C, D, and F in the collection. Do not raise F to F-sharp to fix the tonic into minor. The diminished fifth is the home color. Leave it standing while the figure repeats.
lessons.example: B–C–D–F ostinato, bass on B every bar. The triad B–D–F is diminished and still the tonic. Resolve to C major and you have left Locrian for its relative.
lessons.whyItMatters: Fix the diminished tonic and you leave the mode. Sit on it and the instability is the color you came for.

quiz.stem: Locrian as a tonic hierarchy asks you to sit on which kind of home triad?
quiz.correctAnswer: A diminished tonic already containing a tritone

distractors.text: A major tonic that must cadence through a raised leading tone
distractors.rationale: Locrian's home is diminished, not major.

distractors.text: A power chord with no third, treated as automatically major
distractors.rationale: A fifth stack is not the Locrian tonic triad.

distractors.text: No tonic at all, because modes are forbidden to have a 1
distractors.rationale: Locrian has a 1. That 1 is unstable.

quiz.correctExplanation: Home is already a diminished triad. That is the hierarchy.
objectiveIds: Sit on a tonic whose triad is already diminished

quiz.stem: Why is Locrian unstable as a home and still useful as a color?
quiz.correctAnswer: The tonic triad is diminished, so home itself carries a tritone

distractors.text: The mode has no fifth at all, so nothing can ever sound
distractors.rationale: It has a diminished fifth. That is the itch.

distractors.text: The relative major is legally banned, so color cannot leak
distractors.rationale: The leak into the relative is the usual trap.

distractors.text: Unstable means the kit cannot keep a pulse under it
distractors.rationale: The instability is harmonic, not metric.

quiz.correctExplanation: A tritone inside tonic is why it will not sit still, and why the color bites.
objectiveIds: Predict why Locrian is unstable as a home and useful as a color

quiz.stem: A B Locrian riff starts resolving to C major with a G before it. What happened?
quiz.correctAnswer: The figure left Locrian and cadenced in the relative major

distractors.text: The diminished tonic became more Locrian by landing on C
distractors.rationale: Landing on C is leaving, not doubling down.

distractors.text: Raising F would have been the only way to leave the mode
distractors.rationale: Cadencing in C already left, F-sharp or not.

distractors.text: The mode cannot leave because B is printed on the page
distractors.rationale: Tonic is what the ear treats as 1, not the header.

quiz.correctExplanation: If C becomes home, B is no longer 1. The diminished tonic lost the job.
objectiveIds: Predict why Locrian is unstable as a home and useful as a color

lessons.title: Half-step above the tonic as signature
explanation: Phrygian's signature is the flat second: a half-step above the tonic. E against F, or A against B-flat. That clash is the mode's face, not a wrong leading tone of the relative major. Keep 1 in the bass and let b2 grind against it.

The trap is a secret cadence in the relative major. E Phrygian shares letters with C major. If the riff starts landing on C with a G before it, you left Phrygian. A Phrygian cell stays oriented to E, with F as neighbor rather than as scale-degree 4 of C.
Write E–F–E or E5 against F5 as the cell, then return to E. Do not close on C major. The half-step is the signature only if the tonic still answers as 1 after the grind. Keep the bass honest.
lessons.example: Palm-muted E, then F, then E, open low string as pedal. The half-step is the cell. A last-bar C major triad would steal the tonic and turn F into a neighbor of C.
lessons.whyItMatters: Lose the tonic to the relative major and you wrote a C riff with a flat-2 costume. Keep 1 and the half-step is the signature.

quiz.stem: Phrygian's signature interval against the tonic is which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: The flat second, a half-step above 1, kept as a grind

distractors.text: The raised seventh, used to build a dominant of the tonic
distractors.rationale: That is harmonic minor's leading tone, not Phrygian's face.

distractors.text: The perfect fifth only, with b2 legally banned from riffs
distractors.rationale: b2 is the signature, not a ban.

distractors.text: A rest on beat two, because Phrygian is a meter not a mode
distractors.rationale: The signature is pitch: 1 against b2.

quiz.correctExplanation: 1 against b2. The half-step is the face of the mode.
objectiveIds: Use the flat second against the tonic as a signature

quiz.stem: An E Phrygian cell that secretly cadences in C major has done which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: Left the tonic; F is now a neighbor of C, not a signature against E

distractors.text: Become more Phrygian, because C is the relative and therefore home
distractors.rationale: Relative major as home is leaving, not doubling down.

distractors.text: Proved that Phrygian cannot use F at all without leaving
distractors.rationale: F is the signature against E. C as tonic is the leave.

distractors.text: Changed only loudness, because cadences are mix-fader events
distractors.rationale: The tonic moved. That is a pitch-hierarchy change.

quiz.correctExplanation: Keep E as 1 after the grind. Cadencing in C steals the signature.
objectiveIds: Write a Phrygian cell that does not secretly cadence in the relative major

quiz.stem: Write a two-bar Phrygian cell that does not cadence in the relative. Which keeps E as 1?
quiz.correctAnswer: E–F–E over an E pedal, returning to E without a C close

distractors.text: E–F then C–G–C, so the relative major can finish the phrase
distractors.rationale: That close is the secret cadence this lesson refuses.

distractors.text: C–G–C only, labeled Phrygian because E is in the key signature
distractors.rationale: A C cadence is not an E tonic hierarchy.

distractors.text: E–F#–G# so the half-step is replaced by a major tetrachord
distractors.rationale: F-sharp erases b2, which was the signature.

quiz.correctExplanation: b2 grinds, 1 answers. No C major handshake at the barline.
objectiveIds: Write a Phrygian cell that does not secretly cadence in the relative major

lessons.title: Raised seventh without the classical contract
explanation: Raise the seventh in minor and you get a leading tone plus a minor third: E harmonic minor has D-sharp and G. Common-practice writing uses that D-sharp to build V and cadence. Metal often wants the two colors without hiring the rest of the V–i contract.

The augmented second between the sixth and the raised seventh is a color, not a mistake. Harmonic minor as a default scale is a palette: tonic minor, leading tone, that gap. It is not a promise that every phrase will cadence through a dominant seventh.

Write an E-minor riff that uses D-sharp as a neighbor or a color tone, then returns to E without a B7–Em handshake. Keep the minor third. You took the leading tone. You did not sign the classical cadence clause that usually comes with it.
lessons.example: E–F#–G–D#–E cell over an E pedal. D-sharp bites. No B7. The minor third G stays. The leading tone is a color, not a ticket to a cadence.
lessons.whyItMatters: Take the raised seventh and the whole classical handshake, and you will write cadences the riff did not ask for. Take the color. Leave the contract.

quiz.stem: Raising the seventh in minor without the classical contract means which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: Keep the leading tone and the minor third without hiring V–i

distractors.text: Build B7–Em every two bars, because a raised seventh is a cadence
distractors.rationale: The leading tone can be color without the handshake.

distractors.text: Lower the third to nothing so only the seventh can sound
distractors.rationale: The minor third is half of the default palette.

distractors.text: Switch to major, because a leading tone cancels minor
distractors.rationale: The third can stay minor. That is the point.

quiz.correctExplanation: Leading tone plus minor third. Cadence optional, not included.
objectiveIds: Raise the seventh in minor without taking on the rest of the classical contract

quiz.stem: A metal default that wants the leading tone and the minor third should do which job?
quiz.correctAnswer: Write D-sharp against G over E, without requiring a B7 close

distractors.text: Replace G with G-sharp so the riff becomes E major and cadences
distractors.rationale: That drops the minor third the default wanted.

distractors.text: Avoid D-sharp entirely, because color tones are not material
distractors.rationale: The raised seventh is the material here.

distractors.text: Mute the tonic so only V can be heard as the home pitch
distractors.rationale: Home is still the minor tonic.

quiz.correctExplanation: G stays minor. D-sharp bites. B7 is not owed.
objectiveIds: Write a metal default that wants the leading tone and the minor third

quiz.stem: Someone hears D-sharp in E minor and writes a B7–Em cadence the riff never plays. Predict the error:
quiz.correctAnswer: They took the classical contract with the leading tone, not just the color

distractors.text: They forgot that D-sharp is illegal in any E collection
distractors.rationale: D-sharp is the raised seventh. It is legal as color.

distractors.text: They mixed up loudness with the minor third and muted G
distractors.rationale: The error is a hired cadence, not a mute.

distractors.text: They turned the riff into Locrian by adding a diminished tonic
distractors.rationale: Inventing V–i is a function rescue, not Locrian.

quiz.correctExplanation: The raised seventh arrived. The cadence was extra paperwork.
objectiveIds: Raise the seventh in minor without taking on the rest of the classical contract

lessons.title: Eight notes from alternating steps
explanation: Alternate whole tones and semitones and you get eight pitch classes per octave, not seven. Two flavors: tone-semitone and semitone-tone. Each flavor has few transpositions, because the pattern repeats every minor third and closes on itself.

A diminished-seventh cell lives inside both flavors: four notes stacked in minor thirds. Octatonic collections are symmetrical, so they do not point to one tonic the way a major scale does. Use the set as a closed collection, not as a broken key that needs rescuing.

Build WH starting on E: E, F-sharp, G, A, B-flat, C, D-flat, E-flat. The other flavor starts E, F, G, A-flat, B-flat, B, C-sharp, D. Predict a diminished cell such as E–G–Bb–Db sitting in the first set. Sequence it. Do not correct it into E minor.
lessons.example: WH on E yields E–G–Bb–Db as a ready diminished cell. Cycle it. The collection supplies the other four notes as neighbors. No one tone is the major-scale tonic.
lessons.whyItMatters: Force a major tonic onto a symmetrical set and you will hear a key that the eight notes refused to elect.

quiz.stem: An octatonic collection is built by which interval recipe, and how many pitch classes result?
quiz.correctAnswer: Alternating tones and semitones, eight classes per octave

distractors.text: Seven diatonic steps, then a repeated tonic to fake an eighth note
distractors.rationale: Eight classes, not a doubled seventh scale.

distractors.text: Only perfect fifths stacked until the octave returns
distractors.rationale: Fifths build a different collection.

distractors.text: Random chromatic notes until distortion fills the gaps
distractors.rationale: The recipe is strict: W then H, or H then W.

quiz.correctExplanation: WHWHWHWH or HWHWHWHW. Eight classes. Closed set.
objectiveIds: Build an octatonic collection from alternating tones and semitones

quiz.stem: The two octatonic flavors and a diminished cell inside them are which of these?
quiz.correctAnswer: Tone-semitone or semitone-tone, with a minor-third stack living in both

distractors.text: Major and minor only, with a tonic triad required in each flavor
distractors.rationale: Symmetry does not elect a major tonic.

distractors.text: Pentatonic and blues, with a dominant seventh as the inner cell
distractors.rationale: Those are other collections.

distractors.text: One flavor only, because alternating steps cannot reverse
distractors.rationale: WH and HW are the two flavors named here.

quiz.correctExplanation: Two start-intervals. A diminished tetrachord sits in each.
objectiveIds: Predict the two flavors and a diminished cell that lives inside them

quiz.stem: You sequence E–G–Bb–Db from a WH collection on E. Integrating the set means you should:
quiz.correctAnswer: Keep the diminished cell and the other four neighbors, without electing E minor

distractors.text: Raise Bb to B so the cell becomes an E minor triad plus a leading tone
distractors.rationale: That rescue turns the set back into a key.

distractors.text: Drop to five notes so the collection can count as pentatonic
distractors.rationale: Octatonic is eight. Do not shrink it to fit a nickname.

distractors.text: Add a B7–Em cadence because symmetrical sets still owe V–I
distractors.rationale: The set does not hire a dominant.

quiz.correctExplanation: The cell is the material. E minor would be a different collection.
objectiveIds: Predict the two flavors and a diminished cell that lives inside them
